rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: For the matrix \(\mathrm{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ \lambda & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) to be invertible, the value of \(\lambda\) is :
rows.solution: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero, so expand along the first row: \(\left|\mathrm{A}\right| = 2\left[(2)(3) - (0)(-2)\right] - (-1)\left[(\lambda)(3) - (0)(1)\right] + 1\left[(\lambda)(-2) - (2)(1)\right] = 2(6) + 3\lambda + (-2\lambda - 2) = \lambda + 10\). So A is invertible for every \(\lambda\) except the one that makes \(\lambda + 10 = 0\), i.e. every real \(\lambda\) other than \(-10\). That is option (D) \(\mathbb{R} - \{-10\}\). Note the question asks for ALL admissible values, so a single number such as 0 or 10 cannot be the answer, and \(\mathbb{R} - \{10\}\) excludes the wrong point.

rows.stem: If \(\mathrm{A} = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathrm{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), then value of \(x\) for which \(\mathrm{A}^2 = \mathrm{B}\) is :
rows.solution: Square A first: \(\mathrm{A}^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x^{2} & 0 \\ x + 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Setting this equal to \(\mathrm{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and comparing entries gives TWO conditions: \(x^{2} = 4\), so \(x = 2\) or \(x = -2\), and \(x + 1 = -1\), so \(x = -2\). Only \(x = -2\) satisfies both, so the value is \(-2\), which is option (A) \(-2\). Stopping at \(x^{2} = 4\) is what makes \(2\) and "\(2\) or \(-2\)" tempting; the \((2,1)\) entry is what rules them out.

rows.stem: Let \(\mathrm{f}(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & \sin x \\ \mathrm{p} & -1 \end{vmatrix}\), where p is a constant. The value of p for which \(\mathrm{f}'(0) = 1\) is :
rows.solution: Expand the determinant first, then differentiate: \(\mathrm{f}(x) = \left(x^{2}\right)(-1) - (\sin x)(\mathrm{p}) = -x^{2} - \mathrm{p}\sin x\). So \(\mathrm{f}'(x) = -2x - \mathrm{p}\cos x\), and \(\mathrm{f}'(0) = 0 - \mathrm{p}(1) = -\mathrm{p}\). Setting \(-\mathrm{p} = 1\) gives \(\mathrm{p} = -1\), which is option (D) \(-1\). The value is uniquely determined, so the choice \(\mathbb{R}\) is not available.

rows.stem: If \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3} x^2\, \mathrm{d}x = \mathrm{k}\int_{0}^{2} x^2\, \mathrm{d}x + \int_{2}^{3} x^2\, \mathrm{d}x\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution: Split the integral at \(x = 2\): \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = \int_{-2}^{2} x^{2}\,dx + \int_{2}^{3} x^{2}\,dx\). Comparing with the right-hand side of the given identity, \(\mathrm{k}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx\) must equal \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} x^{2}\,dx\). Since \(x^{2}\) is an even function, \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} x^{2}\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx\), so \(\mathrm{k} = 2\), which is option (A) \(2\). (Arithmetically: \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = \dfrac{27 + 8}{3} = \dfrac{35}{3}\), \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} x^{2}\,dx = \dfrac{8}{3}\) and \(\displaystyle\int_{2}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = \dfrac{19}{3}\), and indeed \(\dfrac{35}{3} = 2 \times \dfrac{8}{3} + \dfrac{19}{3}\).)

Integrate by parts, taking \(\log x\) as the first function and 1 as the second: \(\displaystyle\int \log x\,dx = x\log x - \int x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = x\log x - x\). Evaluating between the limits, \(\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e} \log x\,dx = \left[x\log x - x\right]_{1}^{e} = \left(e\log e - e\right) - \left(1\log 1 - 1\right) = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 1\), which is option (B) \(1\).

rows.stem: The area bounded by the curve \(y = \sqrt{x}\), Y-axis and between the lines \(y = 0\) and \(y = 3\) is :
rows.solution: The strip is bounded by the Y-axis, so integrate with respect to \(\mathrm{y}\). Writing the curve as \(x = \mathrm{y}^{2}\) (from \(\mathrm{y} = \sqrt{x}\)), the required area is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} x\,d\mathrm{y} = \int_{0}^{3} \mathrm{y}^{2}\,d\mathrm{y} = \left[\dfrac{\mathrm{y}^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \dfrac{27}{3} = 9\) square units, which is option (C) \(9\). Integrating \(\mathrm{y}^{2}\) without dividing by 3 produces the distractor 27.

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem:
The order of the following differential equation

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^3\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d}x^3} + x\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^5 = 4\log\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^4\mathrm{y}}{\mathrm{d}x^4}\right)\) is :
rows.solution: The ORDER of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative appearing in it, and it is read off the equation directly, without any regard to how that derivative appears. Here the derivatives present are \(\dfrac{d^{3}\mathrm{y}}{dx^{3}}\), \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx}\) and \(\dfrac{d^{4}\mathrm{y}}{dx^{4}}\), and the highest of these is the fourth, so the order is 4, which is option (C) \(4\). The distractors come from reading other features of the equation: 3 is the highest derivative OUTSIDE the logarithm, 5 is the exponent on \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx}\), and "not defined" is the DEGREE (the equation is not a polynomial in its derivatives, because \(\dfrac{d^{4}\mathrm{y}}{dx^{4}}\) sits inside a logarithm) — but degree is not what was asked.

Substitute \(x = \cos\theta\); since \(\dfrac{1}{2} \le x \le 1\), the angle \(\theta = \cos^{-1}x\) runs over \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right]\), where \(\sin\theta \ge 0\). Then \(\sqrt{3 - 3x^{2}} = \sqrt{3}\sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\theta} = \sqrt{3}\sin\theta\), so the bracket becomes \(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin\theta = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\cos\theta + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin\theta = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \theta\right)\). Because \(\theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), the angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \theta\) lies in \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right]\), which is inside the principal range \([0, \pi]\) of \(\cos^{-1}\); hence \(\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \theta\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \theta\). Therefore the whole expression is \(\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), a constant. (Spot-check at the two ends: at \(x = 1\) it reads \(0 + \cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), and at \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) it reads \(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos^{-1}1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).)

rows.stem: The surface area of a cube increases at the rate of 72 cm\(^2\)/sec. Find the rate of change of its volume, when the edge of the cube measures 3 cm.
rows.solution: Let the edge of the cube be \(x\) cm at time \(t\). Its surface area is \(\mathrm{S} = 6x^{2}\) and its volume is \(\mathrm{V} = x^{3}\). Differentiating the surface area with respect to \(t\), \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{S}}{dt} = 12x\dfrac{dx}{dt}\), and we are told this equals 72, so \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{72}{12x} = \dfrac{6}{x}\). Differentiating the volume, \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{V}}{dt} = 3x^{2}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3x^{2} \times \dfrac{6}{x} = 18x\). At the instant when the edge measures 3 cm, \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{V}}{dt} = 18 \times 3 = 54\), so the volume is increasing at 54 cm\(^{3}\)/sec.

Differentiate once, using the chain rule on the square: \(\mathrm{y} = \left(\tan^{-1}x\right)^{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx} = 2\tan^{-1}x \cdot \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} = \dfrac{2\tan^{-1}x}{1 + x^{2}}\). The key step is to clear the denominator BEFORE differentiating again, so that no inverse tangent survives: \(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx} = 2\tan^{-1}x\). Now differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on the left: \(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\dfrac{d^{2}\mathrm{y}}{dx^{2}} + 2x\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx} = \dfrac{2}{1 + x^{2}}\). Multiplying throughout by \(\left(1 + x^{2}\right)\) clears the remaining fraction and gives \(\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}\dfrac{d^{2}\mathrm{y}}{dx^{2}} + 2x\left(x^{2} + 1\right)\dfrac{d\mathrm{y}}{dx} = 2\), which is the required result.

rows.stem: Find the projection of vector \((\vec{b} + \vec{c})\) on vector \(\vec{a}\), where \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = \hat{i} + \hat{k}\).
rows.solution: First add the two vectors: \(\vec{b} + \vec{c} = \left(\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) + \left(\hat{i} + \hat{k}\right) = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). The projection of a vector \(\vec{u}\) ON \(\vec{a}\) is \(\dfrac{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{a}}{\left|\vec{a}\right|}\) — note the magnitude in the denominator is that of \(\vec{a}\), the vector being projected onto. Here \(\left(\vec{b} + \vec{c}\right) \cdot \vec{a} = (2)(2) + (3)(2) + (2)(1) = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12\) and \(\left|\vec{a}\right| = \sqrt{2^{2} + 2^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 3\). Hence the projection is \(\dfrac{12}{3} = 4\).

rows.stem: An urn contains 3 red and 2 white marbles. Two marbles are drawn one by one with replacement from the urn. Find the probability distribution of the number of white balls. Also, find the mean of the number of white balls drawn.
rows.solution: The marbles are drawn WITH replacement, so the two draws are independent and each has the same composition: 3 red and 2 white out of 5. Writing \(\mathrm{p} = \mathrm{P}(\text{white}) = \dfrac{2}{5}\) and \(\mathrm{q} = \mathrm{P}(\text{red}) = \dfrac{3}{5}\), let X be the number of white marbles drawn, so X takes the values 0, 1 and 2. Then \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X} = 0) = \mathrm{q}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{25}\); \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X} = 1) = 2\mathrm{p}\mathrm{q} = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{12}{25}\) (the factor 2 because the white marble may come on either draw); and \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X} = 2) = \mathrm{p}^{2} = \dfrac{4}{25}\). These sum to 1, as a distribution must. The probability distribution is therefore \(\mathrm{X} = 0, 1, 2\) with probabilities \(\dfrac{9}{25}, \dfrac{12}{25}, \dfrac{4}{25}\). Its mean is \(\sum x\,\mathrm{P}(x) = 0 \times \dfrac{9}{25} + 1 \times \dfrac{12}{25} + 2 \times \dfrac{4}{25} = \dfrac{20}{25} = \dfrac{4}{5}\), which agrees with the binomial shortcut \(\mathrm{np} = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following L.P.P. graphically :

Minimise \(\mathrm{Z} = 6x + 3\mathrm{y}\)

Subject to constraints

\(4x + \mathrm{y} \ge 80\);

\(x + 5\mathrm{y} \ge 115\);

\(3x + 2\mathrm{y} \le 150\)

\(x, \mathrm{y} \ge 0\)
rows.solution: Draw the three boundary lines \(4x + \mathrm{y} = 80\), \(x + 5\mathrm{y} = 115\) and \(3x + 2\mathrm{y} = 150\) in the first quadrant. The origin FAILS both \(4x + \mathrm{y} \ge 80\) and \(x + 5\mathrm{y} \ge 115\), so the feasible region lies on the far side of each of those two lines from the origin; it satisfies \(3x + 2\mathrm{y} \le 150\), so the region lies on or below the third line. No corner lies on either axis: on the Y-axis the first constraint needs \(\mathrm{y} \ge 80\) while the third allows only \(\mathrm{y} \le 75\), and on the X-axis the second needs \(x \ge 115\) while the third allows only \(x \le 50\). So the region is the bounded triangle formed by the three lines themselves. Solving them in pairs: \(4x + \mathrm{y} = 80\) with \(3x + 2\mathrm{y} = 150\) gives \(\mathrm{A}(2, 72)\); \(4x + \mathrm{y} = 80\) with \(x + 5\mathrm{y} = 115\) gives \(\mathrm{B}(15, 20)\); and \(x + 5\mathrm{y} = 115\) with \(3x + 2\mathrm{y} = 150\) gives \(\mathrm{C}(40, 15)\). Each of the three satisfies the constraint not used to produce it, so all three are genuine corners. Since the region is bounded, the minimum is attained at a corner. Evaluating \(\mathrm{Z} = 6x + 3\mathrm{y}\): \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{A}) = 12 + 216 = 228\), \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{B}) = 90 + 60 = 150\) and \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{C}) = 240 + 45 = 285\). The smallest is 150, so the minimum value of Z is 150, attained at \(x = 15\), \(\mathrm{y} = 20\).
